title: Crypto Key Audit – Pseudo Random Number Generation
description: A graded (20-point) hands-on lab based on the SEED 'Pseudo Random Number Generation' lab: audit an insecure time-seeded key generator, recover an encrypted document by brute-forcing the weak key, and learn to generate keys securely from /dev/urandom. Each sandbox has unique flags.
prerequisites: Compiling and running C programs with gcc
Idea of symmetric encryption (AES, keys, IV)
outcomes: Explain why seeding a PRNG with time() produces predictable cryptographic keys.
Perform a known-plaintext brute-force attack to recover a weak AES key.
Measure kernel entropy and explain /dev/random vs /dev/urandom, including a DoS risk.
Generate a cryptographically secure key from /dev/urandom.

levels.title: Introduction
levels.content:
# General information: please read carefully

* This is a **graded** lab worth **20 points** in total. Revealing hints or the solution costs points (each hint shows its own penalty).
* **Every student's sandbox contains different flags.** Copying someone else's answer will not work.
* Submit each flag **exactly** as recovered, without the `FLAG:` prefix or surrounding spaces.
* You also hand in a written lab report (screenshots + explanations), as required by the practical assignment.
* This lab is for educational purposes only. The story is fictitious.

# Storyline

You are a junior security auditor. **HodlerCorp** has hired you after a scare: one of their engineers wrote an in-house utility, `genkey`, to produce the AES keys that protect the company's confidential files. Management wants to know a simple thing — are those keys actually unpredictable?

Your job is to audit `genkey`, **prove** whether its keys can be guessed (by recovering a protected document), and then recommend how the keys *should* have been generated. Everything happens on the SEED Ubuntu workstation in your sandbox.

levels.title: Get access
levels.cloud_content:
Connect to your workstation, then submit the answer **`start`**.

### Sandbox access
1. In the topology view on the right, right-click **`workstation`** and choose **Open GUI**.
2. Log in with username **`seed`** and password **`dees`**.

Prefer a terminal? You can also SSH to the workstation (it makes copy-pasting flags easier). See the [sandbox access documentation](https://docs.platform.cyberrange.cz/user-guide-advanced/sandboxes/sandbox-access/) for setup.

Everything you need is on the **Desktop**.
levels.local_content: This sandbox has not been tested for use with a local sandbox.

levels.title: Task 1 – The developer's shortcut
levels.content:
Open a terminal on the workstation. On the Desktop you will find **`genkey.c`** — the exact program the HodlerCorp engineer used to make 128-bit keys. Read it carefully:

```c
printf("%lld\n", (long long) time(NULL));
srand (time(NULL));          // <-- Line A
for (i = 0; i < KEYSIZE; i++) {
    key[i] = rand() % 256;
    printf("%.2x", (unsigned char) key[i]);
}
```

Compile and run it a few times:

```
gcc -o genkey genkey.c
./genkey
./genkey
```

Notice how the key is tied to the printed timestamp. Now **comment out Line A** (the `srand(...)` line only), recompile, and run it several more times. What happens to the key, and why?

You will see that with no `srand()`, the C library falls back to a **fixed default seed**, so the key comes out **identical every run**. The engineer left a scratch note on the Desktop, **`sample.enc`**, encrypted with AES-128-CBC using exactly that constant key. The IV is:

```
IV = 000102030405060708090a0b0c0d0e0f
```

Reproduce the constant key, decrypt `sample.enc`, and read the note.

**Flag:** the token printed after `FLAG:` inside the decrypted note.
levels.solution:
With `srand()` removed, `rand()` uses the default seed `1`, giving the constant key `67c6697351ff4aec29cdbaabf2fbe346`. Decrypt the note:

```
openssl enc -d -aes-128-cbc -nosalt \
  -K 67c6697351ff4aec29cdbaabf2fbe346 \
  -iv 000102030405060708090a0b0c0d0e0f \
  -in sample.enc
```

The decrypted note ends with the per-sandbox flag token.

hints.title: Which line controls the randomness?
hints.content: Line A — `srand(time(NULL))` — is the only thing seeding the generator. Comment out *just that line*, keep the `rand()` loop, recompile, and compare runs.

hints.title: Getting the key into openssl
hints.content: `./genkey` prints the key as 32 hex characters (ignore the first line — that is the timestamp). Pass it to `openssl` with `-K <hex>`, the IV with `-iv <hex>`, plus `-d -aes-128-cbc -nosalt`.

levels.title: Task 2 – Guessing the key
levels.content:
This is the real audit. On the Desktop is **`secret_report.enc`** — a confidential PDF that HodlerCorp encrypted with a key straight out of `genkey` (so the key was seeded with `time(NULL)`). You are going to recover it with a **known-plaintext brute force**.

What you know:

* The file was created at **2018-04-17 23:08:49 UTC** (epoch **1524006529**). The key was therefore seeded somewhere in the **2-hour window before** that — a Unix-time seed in **[1523999329, 1524006529]** (7200 candidates).
* It is a PDF, so its first 16 bytes are the predictable header:

```
plaintext (16 bytes) = 255044462d312e350a25d0d4c5d80a34
```

* It was encrypted with **aes-128-cbc**, and the IV is stored with the file (never secret):

```
IV = 09080706050403020100a2b2c2d2e2f2
```

* The first 16 bytes of **your** ciphertext (unique to your sandbox):

```
xxd -p -l 16 secret_report.enc
```

Write a program that, for every candidate seed in the window, regenerates the key the way `genkey` does (`srand(seed)` then sixteen `rand()%256` bytes), encrypts the known plaintext block under AES-128-CBC with that IV, and compares the result to your first ciphertext block. When they match, you have the key. Then decrypt the whole file and read the report.

> Tip: `date -u -d "2018-04-17 23:08:49" +%s` prints the epoch seconds, exactly as in the SEED lab.

**Flag:** the token printed after `FLAG:` inside the decrypted report.
levels.solution:
Brute force the 7200-second window. A C solver (OpenSSL EVP) is the canonical approach:

* loop `seed` from 1523999329 to 1524006529
* `srand(seed)`; build the 16-byte key with `rand()%256`
* AES-128-CBC-encrypt the known plaintext block with the given IV
* compare to the first 16 bytes of `secret_report.enc`; on a match, stop

Then decrypt the whole file with the recovered key:

```
openssl enc -d -aes-128-cbc -nosalt -K <recovered-key> \
  -iv 09080706050403020100a2b2c2d2e2f2 \
  -in secret_report.enc -out report.pdf
strings report.pdf | grep -i flag
```

A Python solver using `ctypes` to call libc `srand`/`rand` works equally well. The recovered key and the flag token are different for every student.

hints.title: You already know part of the plaintext
hints.content: Every PDF-1.5 file starts with the same 16 bytes. You have one full plaintext block *and* its matching ciphertext block — enough to test any candidate key without decrypting the whole file.

hints.title: From a timestamp to a list of seeds
hints.content: `date -u -d "2018-04-17 23:08:49" +%s` gives 1524006529. The seed is an integer in [that-7200, that]. Loop over all 7201 values; for each, `srand(seed)` then build the 16-byte key with `rand()%256`.

hints.title: Testing a candidate key
hints.content: For each candidate key, AES-128-CBC-encrypt the known 16-byte plaintext with the given IV and compare to the first 16 ciphertext bytes (`xxd -p -l 16 secret_report.enc`). On a match, decrypt the full file and read the flag.

levels.title: Task 3 – How much randomness does the kernel have?
levels.content:
Good keys need real entropy. Linux harvests it from physical events (key presses, mouse movement, disk and interrupt timing) and tracks an estimate you can read:

```
cat /proc/sys/kernel/random/entropy_avail
```

Watch it move in real time while you use the machine:

```
watch -n .1 cat /proc/sys/kernel/random/entropy_avail
```

Move the mouse, type, read a large file, open a page — and note in your report which activity raises the estimate the most. When you have observed it, run the Desktop helper:

```
./entropy_report.sh
```

**Flag:** the token it prints after `FLAG:`.
levels.solution: `entropy_report.sh` samples `/proc/sys/kernel/random/entropy_avail` and prints the per-sandbox flag. In your report, note that interactive input (mouse, keyboard) and disk activity raise the estimate, whereas a predictable source such as the timer interrupt would not.

hints.title: Where does the entropy estimate live?
hints.content: It is the file `/proc/sys/kernel/random/entropy_avail`. The helper `./entropy_report.sh` on the Desktop reads it and prints your flag.

levels.title: Task 4 – /dev/random, blocking, and a DoS
levels.content:
Linux exposes the random pool through two device files with different behaviour:

* **/dev/random** — a *blocking* device: when the entropy estimate runs out, reads **stall** until the pool refills.
* **/dev/urandom** — *non-blocking*: it keeps producing output from the existing seed.

Experiment (keep a `watch` on `entropy_avail` in a second terminal):

```
cat /dev/urandom | hexdump      # never stops
```

Then answer SEED's question in your report: *if a server reads /dev/random to generate a session key for every client, how could an attacker launch a Denial-of-Service against it?*

The Desktop helper demonstrates the behaviour and gives you the flag:

```
./drain_demo.sh
```

**Flag:** the token it prints after `FLAG:`.
levels.solution: Reading from /dev/random drains the entropy estimate, and the device blocks until the pool refills. A server that calls /dev/random for a session key per client can be stalled by an attacker who opens many connections and keeps the pool empty, denying service to legitimate clients. The recommendation is to use /dev/urandom. `./drain_demo.sh` prints the per-sandbox flag.

hints.title: Blocking vs non-blocking
hints.content: Compare /dev/urandom (never blocks) with /dev/random (blocks when the entropy estimate hits zero). Keep `watch` on `entropy_avail` while you read from each.

hints.title: The attack
hints.content: If every client connection makes the server consume /dev/random, an attacker can keep the pool drained by flooding connections, stalling everyone. Run `./drain_demo.sh` for the flag.

levels.title: Task 5 – Generating keys the right way
levels.content:
Finally, fix the developer's mistake. Instead of a time-seeded PRNG, read directly from the kernel CSPRNG. Here is the secure pattern for a 128-bit key:

```c
#define LEN 16
unsigned char *key = malloc(LEN);
FILE* r = fopen("/dev/urandom", "r");
fread(key, LEN, 1, r);
fclose(r);
```

**Modify it to generate a 256-bit key** (256 bits = 32 bytes), print it as 64 hex characters, then compile and run it. Sanity-check the source's quality with `ent`:

```
head -c 1M /dev/urandom > output.bin
ent output.bin        # expect ~7.99 bits/byte
```

When your program prints a 256-bit key, submit it to the verification oracle on your Desktop:

```
./verify_key <your-64-hex-key>
# or:  ./your_program | ./verify_key
```

**Flag:** the token the oracle prints after `FLAG:` once it accepts a valid 256-bit key.
levels.solution:
Change `LEN` to 32 and print 64 hex characters:

```c
#define LEN 32
for (int i = 0; i < LEN; i++) printf("%02x", key[i]);
```

Compile, run, and pipe to the oracle:

```
gcc -o goodkey goodkey.c && ./goodkey | ./verify_key
```

`ent` on 1 MB of /dev/urandom reports about 7.99 bits/byte (near-ideal). The oracle checks the key is 64 hex characters and that /dev/urandom passes the entropy check, then prints the per-sandbox flag.

hints.title: Which device, and how many bytes?
hints.content: Read from `/dev/urandom` (the non-blocking CSPRNG). 256 bits = 32 bytes, so set `LEN` to 32, read 32 bytes, and print each as `%02x` (64 hex characters total).

hints.title: Getting the flag
hints.content: Run `ent` on 1 MB from /dev/urandom to confirm ~7.99 bits/byte, then submit your 64-hex key: `./verify_key <key>`. It prints the flag once the length and entropy checks pass.
